item.title: desflow from the Command Line: One Model, Every Command
item.description:
A simulation study answers a question about a system by building a model of it and running the model on a computer. Here the system is a shop that packs orders, and the question is whether it needs a third packer. A study goes through the same steps each time: get a model, check that it makes sense, look at what it produces, run it many times, compare the options, and base its inputs on real measurements.

desflow has a command for each step. The previous post said what changed in desflow 0.25.0. This post runs every command on one model and shows what each prints. Everything runs on your own machine, in one folder, without Docker.

item.title: From dynamic-des to desflow: What Changed in Five Releases
item.description:
A simulation is a small model of a real system that a computer plays forward in time. Take a shop that packs orders. Orders arrive at random moments, packers take one at a time, and packing takes longer for some orders than for others. When orders arrive faster than the packers can finish them, a queue forms. A simulation shows how long that queue gets and how long orders wait, without running the real shop.

The last post in this series showed such a model written as a YAML file and run with one command, with dynamic-des 0.16.0 to 0.19.0. The package is now called desflow. It still sends its events to Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, Parquet and Iceberg, and it can now also answer the question a simulation is usually built for, such as “would a third packer keep the wait under 2 seconds?”. Everything below runs on your own machine, without Docker.

item.title: Defining Data-Streaming Simulations in YAML, Without Writing Python
item.description:
A pipeline is easier to test when its input behaves like production: orders arrive at random, queues grow, a machine slows down. A simulation can produce that data, but when the simulation is a Python program, every change is a code change. Someone who only wants to double an arrival rate has to read and edit code, and a reviewer has to check that nothing else moved. A file that holds only settings is easier to read, to compare in a pull request and to run in CI.

desflow 0.16.0 (then named dynamic-des) adds that file. A YAML blueprint describes the whole simulation, and the desflow command runs it. Each of the seven examples in the repository now has a YAML version in plain YAML. The documentation was rebuilt around the three ways to write a simulation.
